newsitem.title: POLAND: Jovial Pope jokes about health, admonishes Poles.
newsitem.headline: Jovial Pope jokes about health, admonishes Poles.

text.p: A jovial Pope John Paul joked with his countrymen on Sunday about still being alive at 77 but sternly warned them of a moral wilderness threatening the freedom they won after decades of totalitarianism.
He also lashed out at criticism of the Roman Catholic Church, calling it Poland's true guardian of liberty.
On the second day of his trip home, the Pope further decried the scandal of "a geography of hunger", urging rich nations to put aside "unrestrained desire for profits" and help the poor.

The Pope, who has suffered from a series of health problems in recent years, appeared tired at the start of the mass before a crowd that police estimated at some 200,000, braving cold drizzle to see Poland's most famous native son.

But he picked up steam during the three-hour ceremony. At the end, he joked about the cool weather, saying he preferred it to the stifling heat of Rome, and set the crowd roaring with laughter when he said: "See, I'm still alive. I just turned 77."
Vatican spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls said the Pope, who marked his birthday on May 18, was "very well," adding: "One can see that he is happy to be home."

In his sermon delivered from a carved wooden throne on an altar platform with a backdrop shaped like breaking waves, the Pope raised his voice almost to a shout, pulling no punches in comments applicable to Poland's political and social debate.
"True freedom demands order," he said. "We are talking first of all about the moral order, order in the sphere of values, the order of truth and goodness.

"When there is a void in the area of values -- when chaos and confusion reign in the moral sphere -- freedom dies, man is reduced from freedom to slavery, becoming a slave to passions and pseudo-values," he said.
Later the Pope made an unscheduled visit to the tomb of Cardinal Boleslaw Kominek, who was made a bishop secretly during the communist years when the church was persecuted.
Leaving the cathedral for an adjacent seminary to address delegates to a Church congress, he broke with his programme to walk about 200 metres (yards) greeting people waiting outside.
In the address the Pope returned to the theme of freedom. "We know the taste of slavery, war and injustice," he said.
"Today we rejoice at freedom regained. But it is impossible merely to possess and enjoy freedom. It must be continually regained through the truth."
Since the fall of communism in 1989, the Pope has often expressed concern that Poland is losing part of its religious heritage as it eagerly embraces social and economic changes.
The Pope is visiting against the background of a domestic political battle centred in part around the role of the Church.

His seventh visit home comes in the midst of a campaign for a general election this year in which rightist opposition parties led by the pro-Catholic Solidarity union hope to supplant the secular-minded ex-communists now in government.
He warned the crowd at the mass of the dangers of a society "permeated by ideas of democracy inspired by liberal ideology".
Last year the ex-communists linked with President Aleksander Kwasniewski relaxed Poland's abortion law, a move which has just been challenged by the constitutional court.
Critics say the Church seeks too much influence. Leftists in parliament have stalled a Concordat treaty with the Vatican regulating such issues as religious education in schools.
Speaking like a stern schoolmaster to a people he considers his children, the Pope rejected accusations by some Poles that the powerful Roman Catholic Church was an obstacle to progress.

"Attempts are being made to convince man and whole societies that God is an obstacle on the path to full freedom, that the Church is an enemy of freedom, that she does not understand freedom, that she is afraid of it," he said.

"This is an unprecedented falsification of the truth," he said. "Saying that the Church is an enemy of freedom makes no sense, especially here in Poland. The Church has proved many times in the last 50 years that it is the guardian of freedom."
The Pope said freedom in Poland and other Eastern European countries "makes the heart beat faster" because it was so hard-won after decades of Nazi and Communist totalitarianism.

"Deep are the wounds that remain in the human spirit from that period. Much time must yet pass before they will be completely healed," said the Pope, who earlier called for reconciliation in Polish society.
Security at the ceremony was very tight, with even priests and nuns going through metal detectors and being frisked.
